motion: Russia is becoming our enemy again

Each side gets thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of direct crossfire. Then each side gets thirty seconds to close. I will give a ten-second cue before each limit, and I will manage interruptions.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Russia is becoming our enemy again because its threats, pressure, and contempt for shared rules are no longer isolated incidents. They shape how we must protect ourselves.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No, pressure is not proof of enmity, and calling-

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That pattern is now strategic, not accidental. It challenges our security, pressures nearby societies, and tests whether we will defend rules that keep smaller countries safe.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, ten seconds.

turns.text: Treating that pattern as harmless would invite more pressure, not peace. That's all, thank you.

turns.text: Thank you, Michelle. And that concludes round one. Now we move on to round two and in round two the debaters address one another directly. You have two and a half minutes, starting when I stop talking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You called the evidence mere disagreement, but pressure on neighbors and repeated threats are more than rhetoric. When conduct steadily targets our security, treating it as hostility is responsible.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that threatening language deserves a firm response. But your main claim turns every confrontation into a return to open enmity, because-

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You are already minimizing the conduct. I am not calling every dispute a war; I am recognizing a pattern that makes peaceful assumptions unsafe, especially when warnings become actions.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If Russia is truly becoming our enemy, why leave room for negotiation at all? Wouldn't your label encourage permanent hostility and make the security problem harder to solve?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A related problem appears in a household protecting its front door. Clear locks, trusted alerts, and agreed signals let families respond quickly without panic, while vague warnings leave everyone exposed and confused.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The motion asks whether Russia is becoming our enemy again, and its conduct supports yes. Negotiation can continue, but it cannot erase threats, coercion, or deliberate pressure against our security.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No state should ever be called an enemy.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant that labels can close doors. But refusing the enemy label in every serious case also blinds us to danger, and Russia's repeated pressure demands a harder judgment.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This state should be called an enemy. Its conduct has crossed from unpleasant disagreement into a direct challenge that deserves the strongest political response available.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm puzzled by your stand. On the one hand no state should ever be called an enemy and on the other hand this state should be called an enemy.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The rule expresses my principle against careless labels, while the case expresses my judgment about this particular state. I still reject the motion because one judgment cannot erase the need for diplomacy.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your distinction does not answer the contradiction: you forbid calling any state an enemy, then call this state an enemy. That retreat from your own rule exposes how serious Russia's conduct is.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The weakest point is your claim that naming an enemy clarifies danger. It can instead simplify a tangled relationship, strengthen hardliners, and reduce the peaceful options you say should remain available.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You say labels create danger, but avoiding an accurate label creates its own danger. Russia's threats and coercion already narrow our choices, so recognizing the enemy trend helps us respond before it deepens.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds to go in this round.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that Russia's behavior deserves resistance. But resistance does not require-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that's time. Okay. Let's all redeem ourselves with our closing statements. So Caroline, you're up first.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The strongest point is the pattern: threats, coercion, and pressure are not isolated disagreements. They show a state acting against our security. We can keep talking, but clear-eyed resistance is wiser than pretending the danger is merely diplomatic friction. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, Caroline, thank you very much indeed. Could I now please ask Michelle to speak against the motion.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The other side's best argument is that repeated pressure forms a pattern. I accept that pattern deserves resistance, but resistance is not the same as declaring a renewed enemy. turns.speaker: MOD

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: We should protect ourselves firmly while keeping communication open. Caution is not weakness; it is the best way to prevent rivalry from becoming lasting enmity. That's all, thank you.
